problem: Prior ImageNav work has no standardized task definition, dataset or benchmark, so methods are hard to compare. Existing formulations have two flaws: goal images are taken at random locations, so they often show walls or hallways and do not identify a place unambiguously, and goal images must match the agent's own camera and embodiment (e.g. the panoramic 360° goals of NTS), which does not fit user-issued goals or narrow-FOV robot sensors.
motivation: The most natural use of image-goal navigation is a user photographing a specific object (e.g. 'my desk') with their own camera, at any height and focal length, and asking a robot to go there. Navigating to specific object instances is also a prerequisite for scene understanding and manipulation. A fully specified public benchmark with a leaderboard lets the community measure progress precisely.
key_idea: Redefine ImageNav as InstanceImageNav: the goal is an image focused on a specific object instance, captured with camera parameters sampled independently of the agent, and success means reaching that object instance rather than the camera pose. The task is released as the InstanceImageNav-HM3D benchmark in Habitat.
insight: The paper frames good goal images as a filtering problem over two coverage heuristics. Object coverage (fraction of the object's observable surface area seen, >0.7) keeps the view unambiguous. Frame coverage (fraction of pixels showing the object, thresholded by an object-size-dependent linear rule) keeps the object prominent while preserving the natural category distribution. The end-to-end model-free RL baseline (RGB-D + goal image + GPS/compass, PPO/VER, 3.5B steps) fits the training set but reaches only 5.5% SR on val. This train/val gap (Fig. 6) shows that instance-level recognition under cross-embodiment goal images does not emerge from sensors-to-action RL alone, leaving the task open for better methods. There are no ablations.
method: Task definition: navigate in an unexplored environment to the specific object instance depicted by an RGB goal image. Reaching another instance of the same category counts as failure, unlike ObjectNav.

Goal-image candidate sampling: a pinhole camera is placed at polar coordinates around the object centroid, with r∈{0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0}m, θ every 10° and height h~U(0.8,1.5)m. It looks at the centroid with pitch/yaw jitter U(−5°,5°) and HFOV~U(60°,120°), decoupled from the agent's camera.

Coverage filtering: frame coverage c_f is the object pixel ratio in a 512x512 semantic mask. Object coverage c_o is the convex-hull surface area of the back-projected mask divided by the total observable surface area pooled over all candidates. Goals are kept if c_o>0.7 and c_f > m*OSA+b (m=0.0232, b=0.02). This leaves 3,667 of 5,347 train objects (69%); an average chair keeps 17 of 178 candidates.

Benchmark instantiation: HM3D-Sem scenes (145 train / 36 val / 35 test) with 6 categories (chair, bed, toilet, couch, plant, TV). Start poses are rejection-sampled so geodesic distance is finite and the geodesic/Euclidean ratio exceeds 1.05. This gives 7,032K train episodes and 2,340 val episodes (3 start poses per object).

Evaluation protocol: success means calling STOP within 0.1m of a valid viewpoint. Valid viewpoints are grid points within 1m of the object's bounding box from which the object is visible with oracle visibility, as in the Habitat ObjectNav challenge. Efficiency is measured with ObjectNav-SPL, taking the shortest path to the nearest valid viewpoint.

Agent embodiment: modeled on Hello Robot Stretch, a 1.41m-tall cylinder with radius 0.17m. It has a forward RGB-D camera at 1.31m (480x640, 58° HFOV) and noiseless GPS+Compass. Actions are MOVE_FORWARD 0.25m, TURN_LEFT/RIGHT 30° and STOP.

Model-free RL baseline: separate ResNet encoders for agent RGB, agent depth and the goal image, plus 32-d linear embeddings of GPS (x,z) and heading (cos,sin). These feed a 2-layer LSTM and a linear categorical action head. It is trained from scratch with PPO + VER on 64 GPUs for 3.5B steps.

setting.backbone: ResNet encoders (text says ResNet-18, equations write ResNet50) for RGB/depth/goal image + 2-layer LSTM policy, trained from scratch with PPO/VER
setting.training_data: InstanceImageNav-HM3D train split: 145 HM3D-Sem scenes, 3,667 object instances, 7,032K episodes. Trained for 3.5 billion steps of RL experience; no extra data.
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D (480x640, 58° HFOV, camera at 1.31m) + GPS+Compass + goal RGB image (independent camera intrinsics/pose)
setting.action_space: low-level discrete MOVE_FORWARD 0.25 m / TURN_LEFT / TURN_RIGHT 30° / STOP
setting.privileged: none (noiseless GPS+Compass provided as a standard sensor)

numbers.extra: 3.5B steps of experience on 64 GPUs; noiseless GPS+Compass
numbers.evidence: Sec. 3.1: "this model achieves a success rate of 0.055 and an SPL of 0.023 on validation, indicating poor generalization"

numbers_note: Only a single baseline number (val SR/SPL) appears in the text. Training-set SR/SPL curves are shown only in Fig. 6 and not reported numerically. No test-split results; the paper says test results will follow via the leaderboard. There are no baseline comparisons against other methods. The architecture text is inconsistent (ResNet-18 in prose, ResNet50 in equations).
results: The paper introduces the InstanceImageNav-HM3D benchmark (7,032K train episodes, 2,340 val episodes, 6 object categories, goal images decoupled from the agent camera). A model-free RL baseline fits the training set but achieves only 0.055 SR and 0.023 SPL on val, showing the task is hard and generalization is poor. No other methods are compared.
limitations: Only a weak end-to-end RL baseline is evaluated; there are no modular, map-based or pretrained-representation baselines and no ablations.
The closed vocabulary covers only 6 object categories; observations and actions are noiseless and only simulation is used.
Goal-image quality relies on hand-tuned coverage heuristics (c_o>0.7, linear c_f threshold), and test-split results are deferred to a future leaderboard.
builds_on: ObjectNav evaluation protocol (Batra et al. 2020, ObjectNav Revisited)
